title: Measurement & Data
description: Comparing, measuring and recording the world: length, mass, capacity, time and money, then data handling from tally charts to statistics and probability. Children measure real things before using formulas.

lessons.title: Which Is Longer?
objectives: Compare two objects by length, height or weight
Use comparison words like longer, taller, heavier
explanation: To find which is longer, line up the ends at the same starting point. The one that sticks out further is longer.
Tall and short are for height — how high something goes. Heavy and light are for weight — how hard something is to lift.
A balance scale shows weight: the heavier side goes down; the lighter side goes up.

vocabulary.meaning: see how things are the same or different

examples: A giraffe is taller than a goat.
A watermelon is heavier than a grape.

story.title: The See-Saw Test
story.text: Momo the bear and Rangi the chameleon sat on a see-saw. Momo's side went down with a bump; Rangi went up high! "You're heavier," giggled Rangi. Then three friends climbed on Rangi's side, and slowly the see-saw balanced.

activities.prompt: On a balance, the heavier side goes…

thinking: Can something big be light? Think of a balloon.
How could you check which of two pencils is longer if they are in different rooms?
speaking: Compare two family members' heights and explain how you checked.

project.title: Coat Hanger Balance

Hang it on a door handle

Say which is heavier and which is lighter

assessment.prompt: Which is longer?
Which is lighter?
To compare lengths, start both at the same line.

mastery: Orders three objects by a measurable attribute

lessons.title: The Order of My Day
objectives: Name times of day and order daily events
Use the words before, after, first, then
explanation: A day has parts. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast. Afternoon comes after lunch. Evening is when the sky gets dark. Night is when we sleep.
Events happen in order. We brush our teeth before bed. We eat lunch after breakfast.
There are seven days in a week: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Then the week starts again.

vocabulary.meaning: when it is dark and we sleep

examples: The sun rises in the morning.
We see stars at night.

story.title: Olu's Upside-Down Day
story.text: Olu the owl sleeps in the day and wakes at night! "Good morning!" Olu hooted as the moon came up. "That's night, silly," laughed Kiko. "For owls, it's our morning!" said Olu. Every animal has its own order of the day.

activities.prompt: How many days in a week?

thinking: Why do you think we sleep at night and not in the day?
What is your favourite part of the day and why?
speaking: Tell a grown-up what you do in the morning, afternoon and evening.

project.safety: An adult should attach the split pin and check that no sharp point is exposed. Keep the pin away from mouths and eyes.

assessment.prompt: Order
Which day comes before Wednesday?
We see the sun rise in the evening.

mastery: Names times of day and days of the week

lessons.title: How Many Hands Long?
objectives: Measure length using non-standard units without gaps or overlaps
Explain why standard units are needed
explanation: We can measure by counting how many of something fit along an object: the table is 8 hand spans long; the rug is 12 footsteps.
To measure fairly, place units end to end with no gaps and no overlaps, starting exactly at one end.
But hands are different sizes! A grown-up's table might be 6 hand spans and yours 9 hand spans. That's why people invented standard units, like centimetres, that are the same for everyone.

vocabulary.meaning: the thing we count when measuring

examples: A pencil is 15 paper clips long.
The door is 4 of Papa's hand spans wide but 7 of mine.

story.title: The King's Bed
story.text: A king ordered a bed 6 feet long, measured with his own feet. The carpenter measured with his smaller feet. The bed came out too short! Then everyone agreed to use the same measuring stick. Now every bed fits.

activities.prompt: A book is ✋✋✋✋✋ long. How many hands?
Everyone's hand span is the same size.

options: They are the same for everyone

thinking: Why did the king's bed turn out too short?
What else could you use as a measuring unit at home?
speaking: Measure a table with your hands and a grown-up's hands, and explain why the numbers are different.

Record each in a table
Ask someone else to measure with their feet and compare

assessment.prompt: A spoon is 📎📎📎📎📎📎 paper clips long. How many?
We should start measuring at the very end of an object.
Measuring with a grown-up's feet and a child's feet gives…

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: O'Clock Times
objectives: Read and show times to the hour and half hour
Identify the hour hand and minute hand
explanation: A clock has two hands. The short hand is the hour hand. The long hand is the minute hand.
When the long hand points straight up at 12, it is "o'clock". The short hand tells which hour: if it points to 3, it is 3 o'clock.
When the long hand points straight down at 6, it is "half past". Half past 3 means the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4.
examples: Long hand on 12, short hand on 7: 7 o'clock.
Long hand on 6, short hand between 2 and 3: half past 2.

story.title: Bolt's Bedtime
story.text: Bolt was told, "Bedtime is at 8 o'clock." At 7 o'clock Bolt looked: the short hand was on 7. "Not yet!" At half past 7, the long hand pointed down. "Nearly!" When the long hand reached 12 and the short hand reached 8, Bolt powered down to sleep.

activities.prompt: Long hand on 12, short hand on 4. Time?
Which hand is the hour hand?
At 9 o'clock, the minute hand points to 12.

thinking: Why do you think the hour hand moves so slowly?
What would happen if clocks had no numbers?
speaking: Show times on a toy clock and tell someone what you usually do at each time.

project.title: Paper Plate Clock

Cut a short and long hand and fix them with a split pin
Show the times of your meals and bedtime

project.safety: An adult should attach the split pin and check that no sharp point is exposed. Use child-safe scissors with supervision.

assessment.prompt: Long hand on 12, short hand on 10. Time?
Half past 1: the long hand points to…
The minute hand is the long hand.

mastery: Reads o'clock and half past times
Shows given times on an analogue clock

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Measuring in Centimetres
objectives: Measure lengths in cm using a ruler
Choose suitable units (cm, m, g, kg, ml, l)
explanation: A ruler shows centimetres (cm). Line up the end of the object with 0 — not with the edge of the ruler — and read the number where it ends.
100 centimetres make 1 metre (m). We use cm for small things like pencils and m for big things like rooms.
Mass is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg): 1000 g = 1 kg. Capacity — how much a container holds — is measured in millilitres (ml) and litres (l): 1000 ml = 1 l.
examples: A pencil ≈ 15 cm; a door ≈ 2 m tall.
A bag of rice: 5 kg; a water bottle: 1 litre.

story.title: The Ruler Mistake
story.text: Kiko measured a crayon starting from the edge of the ruler and got 9 cm. Nova measured from the 0 mark and got 8 cm. "The ruler has a little space before the 0," Nova explained. "Always start at zero!"

activities.prompt: Match the object to the best unit
Where do you start measuring on a ruler?

thinking: Would you measure the distance to school in centimetres? Why not?
Why might a scale show 0 when nothing is on it?
speaking: Measure three things with a ruler and explain how you did it.

project.title: Kitchen Measuring Lab

assessment.prompt: 1 litre = ?
Best unit for a person's mass:
A line starts at 0 and ends at 7 on a ruler. Length?
assessment.why: Measure from zero to the 7 cm mark: the line is 7 cm long.

mastery: Measures accurately to the nearest cm

lessons.title: Tallies and Pictograms
objectives: Record data using tally marks
Make and read a pictogram
explanation: Data is information we collect, like everyone's favourite fruit. We can record it quickly with tally marks: one line for each answer, and every fifth line crosses the other four, making a bundle of 5.
A pictogram shows data using pictures. Each picture might stand for 1 — or sometimes 2 — so always read the key.
We can ask questions about data: Which fruit is most popular? How many more people chose mango than banana?

vocabulary.meaning: shows what each picture stands for

examples: 𝍸 means 5.
Key: 🍎 = 2 people. 🍎🍎🍎 = 6 people.

story.title: The Favourite Fruit Survey
story.text: Zuri asked everyone in Globe Garden their favourite fruit. She made a tally: mango had two bundles of five and two more — 12! Banana had 7, apple 5. Then she drew a pictogram with mango pictures. "Mango wins!" everyone cheered — except Kiko, who loved apples.

activities.prompt: Count the tally: |||| |||| ||| (a bundle of five, another bundle of five, then three)
Mango 12, banana 7. How many more chose mango?
The key tells us what each picture means.

thinking: Why do we cross every fifth tally mark?
Would a survey of 5 people be enough to decide the most popular fruit in India?
speaking: Ask 10 people a question, then explain your results to someone.

Write three things your data shows

Key: 🙂 = 1 child. 🙂🙂🙂🙂 = ?
A pictogram uses…

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Reading a Train Timetable
objectives: Convert between 12-hour and 24-hour time
Calculate durations using timetables
explanation: The 24-hour clock numbers hours from 00 to 23, so there is no need for am and pm. 3:45 pm is 15:45. Midnight is 00:00.
To convert a pm time, add 12 to the hour (except 12 pm, which stays 12:00). 7:20 pm → 19:20.
To find a duration, count on: from 10:45 to 13:20 is 15 minutes to 11:00, 2 hours to 13:00, and 20 minutes more = 2 hours 35 minutes.

vocabulary.meaning: a table showing when things happen

examples: Indian Railways timetables use 24-hour time.
A film from 18:30 to 20:45 lasts 2 h 15 min.

story.title: The Missed Train
story.text: Kiko read "Departs 17:10" and thought it meant 7:10. Kiko arrived at 7 in the evening — two hours late! Nova explained: "17:10 is 10 past 5 pm. Subtract 12 from hours after 12 to get pm times." Next time Kiko was early.

thinking: Why do railways and airlines prefer the 24-hour clock?
If a journey crosses midnight, how do you calculate its duration?
speaking: Explain to someone how you would plan a trip using a real bus or train timetable.

project.title: Plan a Day Trip
materials: a printed or copied bus/train timetable (real or invented)
steps: Choose a departure and destination
Find a train that gets you there before 11:00
Calculate journey time
Plan activities and the return trip, keeping a schedule in 24-hour time

assessment.prompt: From 14:50 to 15:25 is…

assessment.why: Times from 00:00 to 11:59 are in the morning.

units.title: Bar Charts
units.summary: Showing and comparing data with bars.

masteryCriteria: Constructs accurate bar charts with appropriate scales

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Building a Bar Chart
objectives: Draw a bar chart with labelled axes and a suitable scale
Interpret bar charts to answer comparison questions
explanation: A bar chart shows data with bars. The height of each bar shows the amount. Bars should be the same width with equal gaps.
The vertical axis needs a scale — counting in 1s, 2s, 5s or 10s — chosen so the tallest bar fits. Always label both axes and give the chart a title.
Bar charts make comparison easy: we can see at a glance which is biggest and smallest, and calculate differences.

vocabulary.meaning: a reference line on a graph
the numbers marked on an axis
a graph using bars to show amounts

examples: Rainfall in a month: a bar for each week.
Scale in 5s: a bar reaching halfway between 15 and 20 shows 17 or 18 (estimate).

story.title: The Squashed Chart
story.text: Bolt drew a bar chart of cars passing the school: 48, 12, 35. Bolt counted 1 square per car — the paper wasn't tall enough! Rangi suggested a scale of 5 per square. The chart fitted neatly, and everyone could see Monday was the busiest day.

activities.prompt: A chart's values go up to 80. A sensible scale is…
What must every bar chart have?
Bars show 25 and 40. The difference is…

thinking: How could a chart be misleading if the scale doesn't start at 0?
When is a pictogram better than a bar chart?
speaking: Show someone a bar chart and explain three things it tells you.

project.title: Weather Bar Chart

Draw a bar chart with a suitable scale
Write about the warmest and coolest days
Compare week 1 and week 2

assessment.prompt: The horizontal and vertical lines on a graph are…
All bars in a bar chart should be the same width.
If a scale counts in 2s, halfway between 6 and 8 is…

mastery: Constructs accurate bar charts with appropriate scales

units.title: Averages and Spread
units.summary: Summarising data with one number — and knowing its limits.
objectives: Calculate mean, median, mode and range
Choose the most appropriate average for a data set
masteryCriteria: Calculates all three averages and range
Selects and justifies the appropriate average

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Mean, Median, Mode
objectives: Calculate mean, median, mode and range
Choose the most appropriate average for a data set
explanation: An average summarises data with one typical value. The mean adds all values and divides by how many there are. The median is the middle value when values are in order. The mode is the most common value.
The range (largest − smallest) shows how spread out the data is.

Averages can mislead. Five people earning ₹20,000, ₹22,000, ₹21,000, ₹23,000 and ₹5,00,000 have a mean of over ₹1,17,000 — but the median, ₹22,000, describes a typical person far better. Extreme values (outliers) pull the mean.

vocabulary.meaning: a value far from the rest

examples: Data 3, 5, 5, 7, 10: mean 6, median 5, mode 5, range 7.
Shoe shops care about the mode size most.

story.title: The Average Height Trick
story.text: A basketball coach said, "Our team's average height is 160 cm." A rival found that four players were about 140 cm and one was 240 cm! The median was 140 cm. "Choosing which average to report," said Nova, "can change the story."

activities.why: Add the values (20) and divide by 4: the mean is 5.

thinking: Why might a news report choose the mean rather than the median, or vice versa?
Can data have more than one mode?
speaking: Explain to someone, with an example, why the median can be more honest than the mean.

project.title: Family Data Investigation
steps: Collect data from at least 10 people

assessment.prompt: Mean of 10, 20, 30?
An outlier can pull the mean far from typical values.
Middle value when data is ordered:

mastery: Calculates all three averages and range

units.title: Probability
objectives: Place events on a probability scale from 0 to 1

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: How Likely Is It?
objectives: Place events on a probability scale from 0 to 1
Calculate probabilities of equally likely outcomes and compare with experiments
explanation: Probability measures how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). ½ means even chance.
For equally likely outcomes: probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. A fair die: P(rolling a 4) = 1/6. P(even number) = 3/6 = ½.
Experiments give estimates. Toss a coin 10 times and you might get 7 heads. Toss it 1000 times and the proportion of heads usually gets close to ½. More trials give more reliable estimates.

vocabulary.meaning: a measure of how likely an event is, from 0 to 1
how often something happened in an experiment ÷ number of trials

examples: P(sun rising tomorrow) ≈ 1.
A bag with 3 red and 1 blue marble: P(red) = ¾.

story.title: The Lucky Coin
story.text: Kiko tossed a coin five times and got five heads. "It's a lucky heads coin!" Nova tossed it 200 more times: 103 heads, 97 tails. "Short streaks happen by chance," Nova said. "Over many tosses, it's fair."

activities.prompt: Match the event to its probability
pairs: rolling a 7 on a normal die

activities.prompt: After five heads in a row, tails is more likely next.
activities.why: A fair coin has no memory; each toss is still ½.

thinking: Why do casinos always make money in the long run?
Is a weather forecast of "70% chance of rain" wrong if it doesn't rain?
speaking: Explain the "gambler's fallacy" to someone using a coin.

project.title: Dice Experiment
steps: Predict how often each number will appear in 60 rolls
Roll 60 times and tally
Calculate relative frequencies
Combine results with family to make 300 rolls and compare with 1/6

assessment.prompt: Impossible events have probability…
A spinner has 4 equal parts, 1 yellow. P(yellow)?
More trials usually give a better estimate of probability.

mastery: Conducts experiments and compares with theory

units.title: Statistical Thinking
objectives: Interpret scatter graphs and describe correlation
Explain why correlation does not prove causation
masteryCriteria: Distinguishes correlation from causation with examples

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Correlation Is Not Causation
objectives: Interpret scatter graphs and describe correlation
Explain why correlation does not prove causation
explanation: A scatter graph plots pairs of values to see if they are related. If both tend to increase together, there is a positive correlation; if one increases as the other decreases, negative correlation; if no pattern, no correlation.
Correlation does not prove causation. Ice-cream sales and drowning incidents both rise in summer — but ice cream doesn't cause drowning. A third factor (hot weather) drives both.
Good investigations use fair samples. A sample is biased if some groups are more likely to be included — like surveying only people at a gym about exercise habits.

vocabulary.meaning: a part of a population studied

examples: Height and shoe size: positive correlation.
Temperature and heating bills: negative correlation.

story.title: The Firefighter Puzzle
story.text: A student found that fires with more firefighters present caused more damage. "Firefighters cause damage!" he claimed. His teacher asked: what makes a fire need more firefighters? A bigger fire — which also causes more damage. The hidden variable explained it all.

activities.prompt: Match the pair to the correlation
pairs: hours of revision and test score

activities.prompt: Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise. The likely cause is…
A strong correlation proves one thing causes the other.
Surveying only gym members about exercise is…

thinking: How could scientists test whether something actually causes an effect?
Find a news headline that might confuse correlation and causation.
speaking: Explain correlation vs causation to someone using an example you invent.

project.title: Mini Statistical Investigation
materials: a question with two measurable variables
data from 15+ people or a reliable dataset
steps: Write a hypothesis
Plan a fair sample
Collect data and draw a scatter graph
Describe the correlation
Discuss possible confounding variables and whether causation is supported

assessment.prompt: Points sloping down from left to right show…

units.title: Compound Measures
objectives: Calculate speed, distance and time

masteryCriteria: Calculates with compound measures including conversions

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Speed and Density
objectives: Calculate speed, distance and time
Calculate and interpret density
explanation: A compound measure combines two measures. Speed = distance ÷ time. A train covering 300 km in 4 hours has an average speed of 75 km/h.
Density = mass ÷ volume. Water has a density of about 1 g/cm³. Objects denser than water sink; less dense objects float.
Units matter: convert before calculating. 90 km/h = 90,000 m ÷ 3600 s = 25 m/s.

context.text: Pure water at about 4 °C has a density very close to 1 g/cm³; ice is less dense (about 0.92 g/cm³), which is why icebergs float.

vocabulary.meaning: distance travelled per unit of time
a quantity per unit of another

examples: Walk 6 km in 1.5 h → 4 km/h.
A 200 cm³ block of mass 540 g has density 2.7 g/cm³ (aluminium).

story.title: Archimedes and the Crown
story.text: A famous story — reported by the Roman writer Vitruvius centuries later, so historians treat the details with caution — tells how Archimedes checked whether a king's crown was pure gold by comparing the water it displaced with that of pure gold of the same mass. A different volume meant a different density, revealing the fraud.

activities.prompt: An object with density less than water will float in water.

thinking: Why is average speed for a journey not the average of the speeds of each part?
How could you find the density of an irregular stone?
speaking: Explain how density decides whether things float, using examples from the kitchen.

project.title: Density Detectives
steps: Weigh each object
Find its volume by water displacement
Calculate density
Predict and test which will float

assessment.prompt: Time to travel 150 km at 50 km/h?
Density = ?
Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.

mastery: Calculates with compound measures including conversions
